unit.title: Interpret and draw standard electrical drawings

summary: This unit teaches you to read the drawings an electrician works from and to produce simple ones yourself by hand. You will learn the main kinds of electrical drawing, the standard symbols and line types, scales, title blocks, legends and revisions. You will then measure a room and draw its layout to scale, and draw the circuit and wiring diagrams for common lighting and outlet circuits.

blocks.p: Every electrical job starts on paper. The designer shows what is wanted on drawings; you read them to mark out, wire and check the work; and at the end the drawings are corrected to show what was really installed. This unit is for Level 2 trainees. It covers reading the standard drawings used on Jamaican jobs and producing neat, correct drawings by hand with drawing instruments. Drawing with a computer is covered in its own unit, EEMEDR0012B.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Name the kinds of drawing and choose the right one
Tell a layout drawing from a circuit diagram, a wiring diagram, a block diagram and a single-line diagram, and know which one answers your question: where, how it works, or which wire goes where.
Read the drawing sheet
Find the drawing number, revision, scale and date in the title block; use the legend and notes; work only from the latest issue.
Recognise standard symbols

Read the circuit symbols for supplies, switches, lamps, protective devices, meters, motors and components, and the layout symbols for lights, switches, outlets and boards, using the legend when in doubt.
Work with scales and dimensions
Change a measurement on the drawing to a real length and a real length to a drawing length, and know when not to measure a print.
Use drawing equipment
Choose and use the board, T-square, set squares, scale rule, compass, protractor, pencils and template, and look after them.
Measure and sketch a room
Measure a room with a tape and record every size on a neat freehand sketch.
Draw a layout to scale
Draw walls, doors and windows to scale, place the electrical symbols, show which switch controls which light, and complete the border, title block and legend.
Draw circuit and wiring diagrams
Draw one-way, two-way and intermediate lighting circuits and an outlet circuit with correct symbols and conventions, and draw how each terminal is wired.
Use drawings on the job
Follow circuits, count points, apply notes and heights, raise anything unclear, and mark changes so the drawings can become as-built records.

ul: Most new building drawings in Jamaica are **metric**, with sizes in millimetres. Older drawings, and some from designers trained in the United States, use feet and inches. Check which units a drawing uses before you read a single size.

The electrical code used in Jamaica is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**, so many electrical plans use American symbols and words (three-way switch, receptacle, panel). Others use British or international (IEC) symbols and words (two-way switch, socket outlet, distribution board). This kit gives both.
Because symbols differ between offices, **the legend on the drawing always has the last word**. If a symbol is not in the legend, ask before you guess.
Supplies in Jamaica are 110 V and 220 V, 50 Hz. A layout plan usually shows which outlets are 220 V, such as those for a water heater, cooker or air-conditioner, by a note or a special symbol.

blocks.p: Read the sections in order. They start with what drawings are and how to read them, then teach you to draw. Have a scale rule, pencils and paper beside you and try the worked examples yourself. Then try the practice test, and read every explanation, even when you got the answer right.
Different drawings answer different questions. Before you open a drawing, know what you want to find out: **where** things go, **how** the circuit works, or **which wire goes to which terminal**.

head: Drawing
What it shows
What it does not show
Used for
rows: **Layout drawing** (floor plan, lighting plan, power plan)
The building seen from above, drawn to scale, with the positions of lights, switches, outlets, fans, the distribution board and other equipment
How the circuit is connected inside each item
Marking out positions on site, counting items for the materials list, planning cable routes
**Circuit diagram** (schematic)
How the parts are connected so that the circuit works, using symbols joined by straight lines
Where anything is in the building; real cable routes or lengths
Understanding how a circuit works, designing it, finding faults
**Wiring diagram** (connection diagram)
Each terminal of each item and the actual conductor connected to it, laid out much as the equipment is
The building, and often how the circuit works as a whole
Connecting accessories, control panels and distribution boards, and checking connections
**Block diagram**
The main parts of a system as labelled boxes, with lines or arrows showing how they link
Individual wires, terminals or positions
Explaining a whole system quickly, such as a supply, a solar PV system or an alarm
**Single-line (one-line) diagram**
A distribution system with one line standing for all the conductors of each circuit, with the protective devices and their ratings
Each separate conductor (unless marked), or positions in the building
Showing how power is shared out from the supply to the boards and circuits
**Site plan**
The whole plot from above: buildings, roads, the JPS pole, meter position, outside lights and buried cable routes
Inside details of the building
Planning the service and outside cable routes
**Elevation**
One face of a building or one wall of a room, seen straight on
What is behind the wall or inside the room
Heights of windows, wall lights, outlets and switches on that wall
**Section**
A view of the building as if it were cut straight through from top to bottom
The parts in front of the cut
Ceiling and roof spaces, floor levels and wall build-up, so you can plan routes up and over
**Detail**
A small part drawn larger, such as a panel front or a fixing
The rest of the job
Showing exactly how one part is made or fixed
**Panel (circuit) schedule**
A table of the circuits in a board: number, what each supplies, breaker rating and poles, cable size
Positions in the building
Wiring and labelling the board; testing and fault-finding later
**As-built (record) drawing**
The installation as it was really put in, including changes made on site
Ideas that were dropped
Future maintenance, fault-finding, alterations and inspection

blocks.p: Take a bedroom with one ceiling light worked by a switch beside the door. The **layout drawing** shows the light in the middle of the ceiling and the switch beside the door, joined by a curved dashed line. The **circuit diagram** shows the supply, the breaker, the switch in the line conductor and the lamp, with straight lines. The **wiring diagram** shows the switch's two terminals, the lamp holder's terminals and the actual conductor to each. Same light, three different questions answered.

blocks.note: Ask yourself: **Where?** use the layout. **How does it work?** use the circuit diagram. **Which wire, which terminal?** use the wiring diagram. **What is the whole system?** use the block or single-line diagram.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A building job usually comes with a numbered set of drawings: architectural plans, elevations and sections (often numbered A-01, A-02...), electrical drawings (E-01 lighting, E-02 power and so on), a single-line diagram and panel schedules, and the written **specification**. A **drawing register** lists every drawing with its latest revision. When drawings disagree, do not choose for yourself: tell your supervisor.

sections.title: The drawing sheet: paper, title block, legend and revisions

blocks.p: Drawings use the international A-series paper sizes. Each size is half of the one before it, cut across its longer side, so all the sizes have the same shape.

head: Size
Millimetres
Typical use
rows: A0
Large building plans in a design office
A1
Full building plans and site plans
A2
Floor plans of a house or a small building
A3
Room layouts, circuit diagrams, site copies, training drawings
A4
Sketches, schedules, small diagrams, letters

blocks.p: **A3 is twice the size of A4, A2 is twice A3 (four A4 sheets), and A1 is eight A4 sheets.** Drawings are usually laid out **landscape** (wider than tall).

A border line is drawn about 10 mm in from the edge of the sheet, so nothing is lost when it is printed or handled. The **title block** sits inside the border, usually in the bottom right-hand corner, where it is easy to see when drawings are stacked or folded.

head: Title block item
Why it matters
rows: Project name and address, client
Proves the drawing belongs to this job
Drawing title (for example 'Ground floor lighting layout')
Says what the drawing shows
Drawing number (for example E-01)
Each drawing has its own number, so it can be listed, filed and asked for without mistakes
Scale (or NTS)
Tells you whether, and how, sizes can be taken from it; NTS means not to scale
Date
When the drawing was made or issued
Revision letter or number
Which version it is, so you can check it is the latest
Drawn by, checked by, approved by
Who is responsible; a second person checks every drawing
Sheet number (for example 2 of 5)
Shows whether any sheets are missing
Company or Centre name
Who produced the drawing

blocks.p: The **legend** lists every symbol used on the drawing and says what it means. It may also explain abbreviations and line types. You need it because symbols differ from one office, country and standard to another. The **notes** give instructions that apply to the whole drawing, such as mounting heights, cable types, 'all outlets in the kitchen to be GFCI protected' or 'contractor to verify all sizes on site'. Read every note before you start: they are part of the instructions.

head: Abbreviation
Meaning
rows: FFL
Finished floor level: the top of the finished floor, tiles included
AFF or AFFL
Above finished floor (level): for example, 'outlet 450 mm AFFL'
DB, MDB, SDB
Distribution board, main distribution board, sub-distribution board (a panel or load centre in US terms)
CB, MCB
Circuit breaker, miniature circuit breaker
GFCI / RCD
Ground-fault circuit interrupter / residual current device
SP, DP, TP
Single-pole, double-pole, triple-pole (for switches and breakers)
JB
Junction box
WP
Weatherproof
NTS
Not to scale
TYP
Typical: the same detail applies at every similar place
Ø
Diameter
CL
Centre line
REV, DWG, No.
Revision, drawing, number

blocks.p: Drawings are changed during a job: the client asks for something new, the design changes or a mistake is found. Each time, the drawing gets a new **revision** letter or number. A **revision table** above the title block lists each revision with its date, a short description of the change and who made it. The changed area is often ringed with a **revision cloud** (a wavy outline) with the revision letter in a small triangle beside it.

ul: Work only from the **latest revision**. Check it against the drawing register or ask your supervisor.
When a new revision arrives, mark old copies **SUPERSEDED** or remove them from site, so nobody works from them by mistake.
Read the revision table so you know what has changed.
Check the drawing's status. A drawing marked 'preliminary', 'for comment' or 'for approval' is not yet for building from. Work from drawings issued 'for construction'.

blocks.note: Working from an old revision is one of the commonest and most costly mistakes on site. Outlets end up in the wrong place, cables are run along routes that have changed, and the work has to be taken out and done again, at the company's cost.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A building is too big to draw full size, so it is drawn smaller by a fixed amount: the **scale**. A scale of **1:50** means 1 unit on the drawing stands for 50 of the same units on the real job. So 1 mm on paper is 50 mm on site, and the real building is 50 times bigger than the drawing. Everything keeps its shape and its proportions.

head: Scale
Typical use
rows: Small details, such as a fixing or a terminal arrangement
Panel fronts, kitchen and bathroom details, a single wall
Rooms and house floor plans, room layouts in training
Floor plans of houses and larger buildings
Site plans and large buildings

head: You want
Do this
Worked example
rows: The real size from the drawing
Measure on the drawing in mm, **multiply** by the scale number, then change mm to m (divide by 1,000)
At 1:50 a wall measures 66 mm: 66 × 50 = 3,300 mm = **3.3 m**
The drawing size from a real size
Change the real size to mm, then **divide** by the scale number
At 1:100 a 7.5 m wall: 7,500 ÷ 100 = **75 mm** on the drawing
A small item at a large scale
Same rule: real size in mm divided by the scale number
At 1:20 a 450 mm wide panel: 450 ÷ 20 = **22.5 mm**
A site distance
Multiply as before; the answers get large, so take care with the zeros
At 1:200 a cable route measures 37 mm: 37 × 200 = 7,400 mm = **7.4 m**

blocks.note: Check your answer makes sense. A bedroom wall is a few metres long, not 30 cm or 30 m. If your answer is silly, you have probably multiplied when you should have divided, or lost a zero.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **scale rule** has several scales marked along its edges, such as 1:20, 1:50, 1:100 and 1:200. Choose the edge that matches the drawing and read the real size straight off it, in metres, without any sums. Check that you are on the right edge every time.

blocks.h: When not to measure the print

ul: **Always use a written dimension when there is one.** Paper stretches and shrinks with damp and heat, and a copier or printer can enlarge or reduce a drawing without anyone noticing.
A drawing printed 'fit to page' is no longer at the scale written in its title block. A **bar scale** (a short measured line drawn on the sheet) shrinks and grows with the print, so it stays correct.
A drawing or detail marked **NTS** (not to scale) must never be measured. Use only its written sizes, and ask for any you need.
Use a scale rule on a print only for a rough idea, such as planning a cable run; then check on site.

blocks.note: Older drawings and some American-style drawings use feet and inches, with scales such as **1/4 in = 1 ft** (about 1:48) or **1/8 in = 1 ft** (about 1:96). Sizes are written like 12'-6" (12 feet 6 inches). 1 inch = 25.4 mm and 1 foot = 304.8 mm. Never mix the two systems in one calculation.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Line
How it looks
What it shows
rows: Thick continuous
A bold, unbroken line
Outlines and edges you can see, such as the walls of a room
Thin continuous
A fine, unbroken line
Dimension lines, projection (extension) lines, leader lines to notes, and hatching
Thin dashed
A fine line of short dashes
Edges hidden behind something in that view
Thin chain
A fine line of long and short dashes
Centre lines of circles and holes, and lines of symmetry
Chain, thick at the ends
Chain line with bold ends and arrows
Where a section is cut, with arrows showing which way you look
Curved thin dashed (on electrical layouts)
A curved line of dashes from a switch to a light
Which switch controls which light. It is **not** the cable route

ul: **Projection (extension) lines** are thin lines drawn out from the object, with a small gap of about 1 to 2 mm at the object, and running 2 to 3 mm past the dimension line.
The **dimension line** is a thin line between two projection lines, with an arrowhead or a short slanting tick at each end. Building drawings often use ticks.
The size is written above the dimension line, in the middle, so it reads from the bottom or the right-hand side of the sheet.
On metric building drawings sizes are in **millimetres**, written without 'mm' (for example 3600). Site plans may use metres with a decimal point (for example 36.50).
Give each size once only. Give an overall size as well as the smaller sizes that add up to it, so that nobody has to add them up on site.

blocks.p: Symbols are agreed shapes that stand for parts of a circuit or an installation. They make a drawing quick to read in any language. The circuit symbols below follow the international (IEC) style, with the common American alternative where it is different. Layout (plan) symbols vary even more, so always read the legend.

head: Part
How it is drawn
Notes
rows: Conductor
A straight line
Drawn horizontal or vertical, with square corners
Joined conductors
A solid dot where the lines meet
No dot means no join
Crossing, not joined
Two lines crossing with no dot (older drawings: a small hump or loop in one line)
Avoid crossings where you can
Earth (ground)
A short upright line with three horizontal lines below it, each shorter than the one above
A circle round it marks a protective earth terminal
Cell
One long thin line and one short thicker line, side by side
The **long line is positive (+)**, the short line negative (−)
Battery
Two or more cells joined, or one cell with a dashed line between its plates
Mark the voltage beside it
Fuse
A small rectangle with a line running through its length (IEC); an S-shaped curve in American drawings
Write the rating beside it
Circuit breaker
A switch symbol with a small cross on the contact (IEC); a switch with a curved arc over it in American drawings
Write the rating and number of poles
Switch, one-way (single-pole)
A break in the line with a short arm drawn at an angle across the gap
Drawn open (off) unless noted
Two-way switch
One common terminal with an arm that can touch either of two other terminals
Called a three-way switch in American catalogues
Intermediate switch
Four terminals, with two arms that connect them straight through or crossed over
Called a four-way switch in American catalogues
Push button
A switch arm that is pushed onto the contacts and springs back
Used for bells and motor control
Lamp
A circle with a cross (X) inside it
An indicator lamp may be drawn smaller
Bell or buzzer
A bell is drawn as a dome (half circle) on a flat line; buzzers and sirens have similar shapes
Check the legend
Resistor
A plain rectangle (IEC) or a zigzag line (American)
Value in ohms beside it
Capacitor
Two parallel lines of equal length with a small gap between them
A + sign or one curved plate marks a polarised capacitor
Inductor (coil)
A row of small loops, or a filled rectangle
Chokes and coils
Transformer
Two coils side by side, with straight lines between them for an iron core; or two overlapping circles
Mark the voltages, such as 220/24 V
Motor / generator
A circle with M / a circle with G inside
1~ or 3~ under the M shows single- or three-phase
Meters
A circle with a letter inside: V voltmeter, A ammeter, W wattmeter, Ω ohmmeter
A kWh meter is usually a box marked kWh

head: Item
Common symbol
Watch out
rows: Ceiling light point
A circle, or a circle with a cross
A letter beside it (a, b) links it to its switch
Wall light
A circle or half-circle with a short line to the wall
Height given in the notes or beside it
Fluorescent or LED batten
A long thin rectangle, drawn to its length
Length and type in the legend
Ceiling fan
A circle with fan blades drawn on it
May have its own speed control symbol
Switch (American style)
The letter S; S3 for a three-way and S4 for a four-way switch
British-style plans use small circles with short strokes instead
Outlet, 110 V duplex (American style)
A small circle with two short parallel lines through it
A note or subscript shows special outlets
Special outlets
The outlet symbol marked GFCI, WP, 220 V, or a separate symbol
Check the legend: 220 V outlets must not be confused with 110 V ones
Distribution board (panel)
A rectangle, often half or wholly filled in, labelled DB or Panel A
The board name matches the panel schedule
Water heater, A/C, exhaust fan
A box or circle with letters such as WH, A/C, EF
Usually fed by their own circuit
Bell push, data, telephone, smoke detector
Small special symbols
Always in the legend

blocks.note: The same shape can mean different things on different drawings. A circle with a cross is a lamp on a circuit diagram but may be a junction box on another office's plan. **Never guess: read the legend.**
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Lighting and outlet circuits on paper

head: Conductor
What it does
rows: Line (L), live, hot
Brings the supply from the breaker. Switches and fuses always go in the line.
Neutral (N)
Carries the current back to the source. It is never switched by an ordinary light switch.
Earth (E), ground, protective conductor
Connects metal parts back to the board so that a fault trips the breaker.
Switch wire (switched line, switch leg)
Runs from the switch to the lamp. It is live only when the switch is on.
Strappers (travellers)
The two conductors that join a pair of two-way switches, and pass through any intermediate switch.
Common (COM)
The terminal of a two-way switch that connects to either strapper terminal in turn.

flow: Supply line from the breaker
One-way switch
Switch wire
Lamp
Neutral back to the board

blocks.p: The switch must be in the **line** conductor. If it were in the neutral, the lamp would go out, but the lampholder would still be live when the switch was off, and the person changing the lamp could get a shock. Show the earth conductor to the light point and to a metal switch box.

**Two or more lamps on one switch** are drawn in **parallel**: the switch wire goes to each lamp, and a neutral returns from each lamp. If one lamp fails, the others stay lit, and each lamp gets the full supply voltage.

flow: Line to COM of switch 1
Two strappers from switch 1 to switch 2
COM of switch 2
Switch wire to the lamp
Neutral back to the board

blocks.p: Used for stairs and long rooms with two doors. Changing **either** switch changes the lamp from off to on, or on to off.

Keep a two-way switch at each end, and put an **intermediate switch** in the strappers for each extra switching point. An intermediate switch either passes the strappers straight through or crosses them over, so working it also changes the lamp. Three places need one intermediate; four places need two; and so on.

head: Switching points
British (IEC) names
American (NEC catalogue) names
rows: One one-way switch
One single-pole switch
Two two-way switches
Two three-way switches
Two two-way switches + one intermediate
Two three-way switches + one four-way
Two two-way switches + two intermediates
Two three-way switches + two four-ways

blocks.p: A radial outlet circuit runs from its breaker to the first outlet, then on to each outlet in turn, ending at the last one. Line, neutral and earth are each drawn going to every outlet. Show the breaker rating and the cable size beside the circuit.

blocks.h: How a layout drawing shows circuits

ul: A **curved dashed line** from a switch to a light shows which switch controls it. The real cable route is decided on site or shown separately.
**Letters** beside lights and switches (a, b, c) show which switch works which lights when lines would clutter the drawing.
An **arrowhead** on a cable line marked with a board and circuit number, such as 'DB-A 5', shows the circuit runs back ('home run') to board A, circuit 5.
**Short strokes** across a cable or conduit line can show how many conductors it carries: three strokes means three conductors. The legend explains the marking used.

blocks.h: Single-line diagram of a small board

blocks.p: A house in Jamaica might be shown like this, one line for each circuit:

flow: JPS service
Meter (kWh)
Main breaker, two-pole
Board busbars
Branch breakers, each labelled with its rating, poles and circuit number

blocks.p: For example: circuit 1, lights, 15 A single-pole; circuit 3, kitchen outlets, 20 A single-pole; circuits 2 and 4, water heater, 30 A two-pole (220 V). These ratings are examples only: the designer chooses them for each job. The grounding electrode (earth rod) and main earthing conductor are shown at the service.

head: Equipment
Used for
Care
rows: Drawing board
A flat, smooth surface with a straight edge for the T-square
Keep it clean and dry; do not cut on it
T-square
Sliding along the board's edge to draw **horizontal** lines, and as a base for the set squares
Keep the edge straight and clean; never use it as a hammer or cutting guide
Set squares: 45° and 30°/60°
Resting on the T-square to draw **vertical** lines and lines at 30°, 45° and 60°
Keep the edges free of nicks; store flat
Scale rule
Measuring and drawing to scale without sums
Do not use it as a straight edge for a knife
Compass
Drawing circles and arcs, such as door swings
Keep the point and lead sharp and the joint firm
Protractor
Measuring and drawing angles
Store flat so it does not crack
Symbol template (stencil)
Drawing symbols neatly and all the same size
Wash it; keep it flat
Pencils
Construction lines, lining in, lettering
Keep them sharp
Eraser and eraser shield
Rubbing out; the shield protects lines you want to keep
Keep the eraser clean
Masking tape or clips
Holding the paper square on the board
Tape removes cleanly; drawing pins leave holes
French curve
Drawing smooth curves that are not part of a circle
Store flat

blocks.p: Pencils run from hard (H) to soft (B). The higher the number before H, the harder the lead and the fainter and finer its line. The higher the number before B, the softer and darker the line.

head: Grade
Line
Use
rows: 2H, 3H
Hard, light, fine
Construction (guide) lines that will be lined in or rubbed out
H, F
Medium-hard, clean
Lining in on smooth paper
HB
Medium, dark enough to copy
Lining in, lettering and sketching
B, 2B
Soft, dark, smudges easily
Freehand sketching and shading; not for fine drawing

ul: Use **clear capital letters** of an even size: about 3 to 5 mm for notes and labels, and 5 to 7 mm for titles.
Draw two faint guide lines with the 2H pencil so all letters are the same height.
Keep letters upright, evenly spaced and dark enough to read on a copy.
Write so the text reads from the bottom of the sheet (or the right-hand side for vertical dimensions).

blocks.note: Wash your hands before drawing and keep a sheet of clean paper under your hand. Graphite smudges are the most common reason a good drawing looks untidy.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Measuring a room and sketching it

flow: Walk round the room and make a freehand sketch of its shape, large enough to write on
Measure each wall with a tape, corner to corner, and write each size on the sketch at once
Measure the position and width of each door and window from a corner, and the way each door opens
Measure the wall thickness at a door opening
Mark the position of each light, switch, outlet, board and fixed item, measured from a corner
Check: do the parts of each wall add up to its overall length?

blocks.note: Watch for trip hazards and wet floors while you measure, and do not enter a workshop bay while machines are running. Do not open any board, outlet or switch to see inside: draw only what you can see.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Choose the scale and paper so the room fits with space for the title block and legend
Fix the paper square on the board with masking tape
Draw the border and the title block outline
Draw the walls lightly (2H) to scale with the scale rule, T-square and set squares
Add doors (with their swing), windows and fixed items
Place the electrical symbols, using the template
Add switch-to-light lines, notes, dimensions and the legend
Line in (HB), letter the drawing and complete the title block
Check the drawing against the sketch and the room

blocks.p: Drawing lightly first lets you correct mistakes before they are permanent. Line in only when the whole layout is right.

ul: Put the supply on the left or at the top, and let the circuit read from left to right or top to bottom.
Draw conductors as straight horizontal and vertical lines with square corners. Do not draw the real cable routes.
Arrange the symbols so that lines cross as little as possible.
Put a solid dot at every real join, and nowhere else.
Show switches and contacts in their off (open) position unless the drawing says otherwise.
Label conductors L, N and E, and give each part a name or number and a rating.
Add a title, legend and drawing number.

blocks.h: Drawing a wiring diagram from a board

flow: Confirm with the instructor that the board is not connected to any supply
Start at the board's breaker for your circuit
Follow each conductor by eye to the first accessory, without touching any terminal
Note the name or marking of each terminal (L, N, E, COM, L1, L2) and which conductor goes to it
Make a rough sketch as you go, then go on to the next accessory
Draw the neat wiring diagram, with each terminal and each conductor, using colour pencils to match the conductors
Draw the matching circuit diagram from the wiring diagram
Ask another person to check both drawings against the board

ul: Every item on the sketch or board is on the drawing, and nothing extra.
Each symbol matches the legend, and each item is in the right place.
Switches are in the line conductor; every circuit is complete back to the supply.
Junction dots only at joins; labels and ratings present.
Scale, title, number, date, revision and your name are in the title block.
Lettering is clear and the sheet is clean.

head: Points
By hand
With CAD software
rows: Good points
Cheap; needs no power or computer
Quick for sketches on site
Teaches how a drawing is built
Accurate; changes are quick
Symbol libraries reuse the same symbols
Saved, printed at any scale and emailed
Weak points
Changes mean rubbing out and redrawing
Copies must be printed or scanned
Needs a computer, software and training
Files can be lost without backups

sections.title: Reading and using drawings on the job

flow: Check the title block: right job, right drawing, latest revision, issued for construction
Note the scale, and any part marked NTS
Read the legend and every note
Find a known point (the main door, the north point, a column) and turn the drawing to match the building
Follow each circuit from the board to every point
Count the items and list the materials
Ask your supervisor about anything unclear before you start

blocks.p: A power layout shows, in one shop: 8 duplex outlets, 2 outlets marked GFCI, 1 outlet marked 220 V for an air-conditioner, and 3 data points. The electrical items to order are 8 + 2 + 1 = **11 outlets of three kinds** (8 ordinary, 2 GFCI, 1 220 V) and the boxes for them. The data points are usually for another trade: check the specification. Count each kind separately, because each needs different materials.

Heights are given in the notes or beside the symbol, measured from the finished floor level (FFL). A general note such as 'outlets 450 mm AFFL unless noted otherwise' applies everywhere, **except** where a different height is written beside an item: then the written height wins. Typical figures you will see are outlets about 300 to 450 mm and switches about 1,100 to 1,200 mm above the finished floor, with kitchen counter outlets higher, but always follow the drawing. Measure from the **finished** floor: if the tiles are not yet laid, allow for their thickness.

blocks.h: When the drawing does not match the site

ul: A wall, beam or window is not where the drawing shows it: stop and tell your supervisor.
Two drawings, or a drawing and the specification, disagree: do not pick one; report it.
A symbol is not in the legend or a note is unclear: ask.
Any change is approved by the supervisor or designer before it is done, and then recorded.

blocks.p: When an approved change is made on site, mark it on the site copy in a clear colour (often red), with the date and your initials, and tell your supervisor. A quick freehand sketch is a good way to record a change at once, but it does not replace the drawing: pass it on so the change is approved and added. At the end of the job the marked-up copies are used to produce the **as-built (record) drawings**, which show exactly what was installed. They protect the next person who works there: someone drilling a wall or digging a trench needs to know where the cables really are.

ul: Keep site copies in one set place, flat or rolled in a tube, not folded into pockets.
Protect them from rain, sun and dust: use a plastic sleeve or a clipboard cover. Jamaican sun fades prints quickly and a sudden shower can ruin a set.
Do not write on the master copy; mark changes only as described above.
Return drawings to the site office or the file at the end of the day.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, a new or altered installation must be inspected and certified before JPS connects it. The inspector compares the work with the approved drawings and the code, so drawings that match the work make inspection quicker.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can say what a layout drawing, circuit diagram, wiring diagram, block diagram, single-line diagram, site plan, elevation and section each show, and choose the right one for a question.
I can find the drawing number, scale, date and revision in a title block and explain why each matters.
I can explain why only the latest revision is used and what happens to old copies.
I can use the legend and notes, and explain common abbreviations such as FFL, AFFL, DB, NTS and TYP.
I can convert between drawing sizes and real sizes at 1:20, 1:50, 1:100 and 1:200, and I know when to use written sizes instead.
I can name and draw the main line types and dimension a drawing correctly.
I can draw and recognise the standard symbols for circuit diagrams and layout plans.
I can draw one-way, two-way and intermediate lighting circuits and a radial outlet circuit, with switches in the line.
I can give the British and American names for two-way and intermediate switches.
I can choose and use drawing instruments and pencil grades, and look after them.
I can measure a room, sketch it with sizes and draw its layout to scale with a title block and legend.
I can draw a wiring diagram and a circuit diagram from a board without touching it.
I can check a drawing, raise problems with my supervisor and record approved changes for the as-built drawings.

terms: As-built drawing
A drawing corrected at the end of a job to show the installation as it was really put in.
Bar scale
A measured line drawn on the sheet; it stays correct when the drawing is enlarged or reduced.
Block diagram
A drawing of a system as labelled boxes joined by lines, showing the main parts and how they link.
Circuit diagram (schematic)
A drawing that uses symbols to show how a circuit's parts are connected and how it works, not where they are.
Elevation
A view of one face of a building or one wall of a room, seen straight on.
FFL / AFFL
Finished floor level / above finished floor level, used for mounting heights.
Intermediate switch
A four-terminal switch placed in the strappers between two two-way switches; a four-way switch in American catalogues.
Layout drawing
A scaled plan of a building showing where the lights, switches, outlets and equipment are placed.
Legend (key)
The list on a drawing of every symbol and what it means.
NTS
Not to scale: the drawing must not be measured.
Revision
A new version of a drawing, shown by a letter or number in the title block and listed in the revision table.
Scale
The fixed ratio between a drawing and the real object, such as 1:50.
Section
A view of a building as if cut straight through, showing the inside.
Single-line diagram
A diagram of a distribution system in which one line stands for all the conductors of a circuit.
Strappers (travellers)
The two conductors that join two-way switches.
Superseded
Replaced by a later revision and no longer to be used.
Switch wire
The conductor from a switch to the lamp, live only when the switch is on.
Title block
The box on a drawing giving its title, number, scale, date, revision and the names of those responsible.
Two-way switch
A switch with a common terminal that connects to either of two strapper terminals; a three-way switch in American catalogues.
Wiring diagram
A drawing that shows each terminal and the conductor connected to it, as the item is really wired.

c1.title: Classroom block drawings in Port Antonio
c1.text: Trainee Akeem Lewis is working with electrician Mrs Beverley Dawkins on a new two-classroom block at a high school in Port Antonio, Portland. The lighting layout is drawing E-01, drawn at 1:100 on an A3 sheet. The copy pinned up in the site office is Rev B; the office has just emailed Rev C, whose revision table says 'Switch heights changed; outlet O7 moved'. A general note on E-01 reads: 'Switches 1200 mm AFFL unless noted otherwise.'

c2.title: A guest cottage bedroom in Negril
c2.text: Trainee Shanique Brown has been asked to draw, by hand, the electrical layout of a guest cottage bedroom in Negril, Westmoreland. The room measures 4.2 m by 3.6 m and has one door and one window. It has a ceiling fan with a light, two switches beside the door, four outlets and an outlet for an air-conditioner. Her supervisor wants the layout at 1:50 on an A3 sheet, with a border, title block and legend.

c3.title: Stair lighting in a Falmouth church hall
c3.text: A church hall in Falmouth, Trelawny, has a staircase up to a gallery. Electrician Mr Courtney Walters wants the landing light to be switched from the foot of the stairs, the top of the stairs and the gallery door. Trainee Romario Gayle must draw the circuit diagram before any cable is pulled. The light is fed from a 15 A breaker in the hall's panel.

c4.title: A pump control panel at a Junction farm
c4.text: At a farm near Junction, St Elizabeth, an irrigation pump is run from a control panel in a block pump house. A block diagram on the panel door shows: JPS supply, meter, main disconnect, control panel, pump. Inside are a contactor, an overload relay, a small control transformer and a terminal strip, with an old wiring diagram taped to the door. Electrician Mrs Sonia Facey and trainee Dameon Hall must replace the contactor and update the drawings, because the pump was moved last year to a new well.

c5.title: A clinic extension in Port Maria
c5.text: Trainee Kerry-Ann Thompson is helping to wire an extension to a clinic in Port Maria, St Mary. The architect's set includes a floor plan, a front elevation and a section through the new waiting room, all at 1:50, and a detail of the reception desk marked 'NTS'. During the job the nurse in charge asks for an extra outlet behind the desk, and Kerry-Ann makes a quick freehand sketch of where it should go.

questions.q: Akeem is about to mark out the switch positions from the Rev B copy on the office wall. What should Mrs Dawkins tell him?
o: Mark out from Rev B, as only one outlet was moved in Rev C
Use Rev C, and mark the Rev B copy superseded or take it down
Mark out from Rev B now and check the Rev C changes at the end
Use both copies and pick whichever height looks better on site
questions.why: Only the latest revision may be worked from. Rev C changed the switch heights, so every switch marked from Rev B would be wrong. Old copies are marked superseded or removed so that nobody else uses them by mistake.

questions.q: On E-01 the corridor measures 64 mm with a scale rule, and no size is written along it. About how long is the real corridor?
questions.why: At 1:100, multiply the drawing size by 100: 64 × 100 = 6,400 mm = 6.4 m. Because no size is written, a scaled measurement is a fair guide, but check it on site before cutting or ordering anything.

questions.q: In the staff room, E-01 shows one switch with '1050 AFFL' written beside it. At what height should that switch be fitted?
o: 1050 mm above the finished floor, as written beside it
1200 mm, because the general note covers every switch
1125 mm, halfway between the note and the written marking
1200 mm, as the 1050 marking must be for an outlet
questions.why: 'Unless noted otherwise' means the general height applies everywhere except where a different height is written beside an item. A height written beside a symbol overrides the general note.

questions.q: On the power layout, a cable line from an outlet ends in an arrowhead marked 'DB-A 5'. What does this usually show?
o: Five cables must be pulled into that length of conduit
The outlet is to be fitted 5 m from distribution board A
The circuit runs back to board DB-A as circuit number 5
The outlet must wait until board A has five circuits
questions.why: An arrowhead with a board name and number is a 'home run': it shows which board and which circuit the cable goes back to. The panel schedule for DB-A will list circuit 5 and its breaker.

questions.q: How long should Shanique draw the 4.2 m wall at a scale of 1:50?
o: 42 mm
84 mm
8.4 mm
210 mm
questions.why: Change to millimetres and divide by the scale number: 4,200 ÷ 50 = 84 mm. A quick check: at 1:50, every metre is 20 mm on paper, and 4.2 × 20 = 84.

questions.q: Her supervisor asks how big the room would be if it were drawn at 1:20 instead. What size would the 4.2 m by 3.6 m room be on paper?
o: 84 mm by 72 mm
420 mm by 360 mm
21 mm by 18 mm
210 mm by 180 mm
questions.why: Divide each real size in millimetres by 20: 4,200 ÷ 20 = 210 mm and 3,600 ÷ 20 = 180 mm. That would fill most of an A3 sheet (420 × 297 mm), leaving little room for the title block and legend, which is why 1:50 was chosen.

questions.q: Which instruments should Shanique use to draw the vertical lines of the walls?
o: A set square resting on the edge of the T-square
The T-square on its own, turned up on its short end
A compass opened out to the length of the wall
A protractor set at 90° along the paper's edge
questions.why: The T-square slides on the board's edge and gives horizontal lines. A set square resting on the T-square gives true vertical lines, and lines at 30°, 45° and 60°.

questions.q: Shanique wrote only the length and width of the room on her sketch. What else must she measure before she can draw the layout?
o: The rating of the breaker that feeds the A/C outlet
The length of cable from the board to each outlet
The height of the fan blades above the bed
The door, window and each outlet, from a corner
questions.why: A layout shows where things are, so she needs the position and width of the door and window and the position of every electrical item, measured from a fixed corner. Breaker ratings and cable lengths are not needed to draw the layout.

questions.q: Mr Walters then asks for a fourth switching point at the vestry door. How does this change Romario's diagram?
o: A second intermediate switch goes between the two-way switches
A third two-way switch is added beside the first two-way switch
The two-way switches are changed for four one-way switches
A one-way switch is added in the neutral to the lamp
questions.why: However many switching points there are, there is a two-way switch at each end and one intermediate switch for each extra point in between. Four points need two two-way switches and two intermediates.

questions.q: The supplier's catalogue is American. What should Romario look for to buy the intermediate switches?
o: Three-way switches
Four-way switches
Double-pole switches
Single-pole switches
questions.why: American names count terminals: the British two-way switch is a 'three-way' switch, and the British intermediate is a 'four-way' switch. A double-pole switch breaks two conductors at once and is not the same thing.

questions.q: Romario's first draft puts the switches in the neutral and runs the line straight to the lamp. What is wrong with this?
o: The lamp would glow at half brightness all the time
The breaker would trip each time a switch was used
The lampholder would stay live with the light off
Nothing, as long as every switch used is two-way
questions.why: Switching the neutral still turns the lamp off, but the line stays connected to the lampholder. Someone changing the lamp with the light 'off' could get a shock. Switches always go in the line conductor.

questions.q: The landing light is on. Someone works the intermediate switch at the top of the stairs. What happens, and why?
o: Nothing, as an intermediate needs a third switch to act
The light goes off, as the strappers are crossed over
The breaker trips, as the line is joined to the neutral
The light stays on but now at a lower brightness
questions.why: An intermediate switch either passes the two strappers straight through or crosses them over. Changing it moves the supply to the other strapper, so the light changes state, just as it does when either two-way switch is worked.

questions.q: What can the block diagram on the panel door NOT tell Dameon?
o: That the main disconnect comes before the panel
The order in which the supply reaches the pump
Which conductor goes to each contactor terminal
That the pump is fed from the control panel
questions.why: A block diagram shows the main parts of a system and how they link, as boxes. It does not show terminals or conductors; for that you need the wiring diagram.

questions.q: On the single-line diagram Mrs Facey draws, the pump cable is one line with three short strokes across it. What do the strokes show?
o: The cable route is three metres long
The cable has three joins along its length
The cable has three conductors in it
The cable must be tested on three days
questions.why: On a single-line diagram one line stands for all the conductors of a circuit. Short strokes across the line show how many conductors there are. The legend confirms the marking used on that drawing.

questions.q: On the farm's site plan, drawn at 1:500, the cable route to the new well measures 82 mm. How long is the route on the ground?
questions.why: Multiply by the scale number: 82 × 500 = 41,000 mm = 41 m. With large scale numbers it is easy to lose a zero, so check that the answer is sensible for a farm.

questions.q: The old drawings still show the pump cable going to the old well. Why does this need correcting?
o: Someone digging later could hit a cable not on the drawing
The pump would run more slowly than its nameplate says
The meter would record more units than the pump uses
The overload relay would trip every time the pump started up
questions.why: Drawings are only useful if they show what is really there. A worker digging or a contractor laying pipes relies on the drawing to know where buried cables are. Correcting the drawings produces an as-built record.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann wants to know how much space there is between the ceiling and the roof for cable runs. Which drawing should she look at?
o: The section through the waiting room
The floor plan of the waiting room
The front elevation of the building
The NTS detail of the reception desk
questions.why: A section shows the building as if cut through from top to bottom, so it shows the ceiling, the roof space and the roof. A floor plan shows only the view from above, and an elevation shows only the outside face.

questions.q: On the NTS desk detail, a cable entry measures 25 mm with her scale rule. How should Kerry-Ann find its real size?
o: Multiply 25 mm by 50, as the other sheets are at 1:50
Multiply 25 mm by 100, as most details are at 1:100
Use only the written sizes, and ask for any not shown
Measure it twice and use the average of the readings
questions.why: NTS means not to scale, so measuring the print gives a meaningless answer. Use only the sizes written on the detail, and ask the supervisor or designer for any size that is missing.

questions.q: What should happen to Kerry-Ann's freehand sketch of the extra outlet?
o: She keeps it in her pocket as her own record
It is used in place of the drawing, as it is newer
It is thrown away once the outlet has been fitted
It goes to the supervisor to approve and record
questions.why: A sketch is a quick way to record a change, but it does not replace the drawing. The supervisor approves the change, and it is marked on the drawings so that the as-built record is complete.

questions.q: A layout must be printed on A2 paper. How many A4 sheets would cover the same area as one A2 sheet?
o: Two
Eight
Six
Four
questions.why: Each A size is half the one before it: A3 is two A4 sheets, so A2 (two A3 sheets) is four A4 sheets. A2 measures 420 × 594 mm.
